title: Leaving the band in Chicago and where the members went
summary: He came home alone, leaving the band in Chicago; reflections on age; Roy, Lawrence Dewey and Eddie Garland now.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: I left the whole bank. The only one came home. And I left them all there and I even give them the, give them the, if they want the ticket, they can have it to go back home. And they said, no, they ain't coming. I said, well, all right. So I got my ticket and I told the manager, I says, give them the money. And they got the money and I just came back home with my ticket. See, I got my pay and I said, well, there's your money. So who ain't coming home with me? I'm going by myself. So I got a telegram to come back again. But I just naturally say, well, I didn't care about it because I feel like I was getting old and I couldn't do like I used to, you know. You know, when you get a certain age, you can't, you imagine you can do it. But that old imagination don't get it. See, imagination. I see some old man, 90 years old, they want some young women, 15, 18 years old. Well, you know you can't make it, you know. I see them all the time. I see some of them on the television. Of course, I understand them and it's a funny thing, you know. And imagination. Because sometimes you think you can do like you used to do years back. And then, you know, you get shame of your own self. And you'll be shamed by someone else too. So I rather who fall down stay down. Stay on your stay. Like the old boys say, the old songs say. Stay in your own backyard. Don't worry about the other fellow, what he doing. You heard that song? Yeah. Mama stay in your own backyard. Don't worry about what the other fellow is doing. So finish then. Now, Roy, he was, he was, he went to work over there somewhere to tell me, in some stock yard.
I think he worked in steel mills for the last I knew. He was working, he was a mechanic too, I think, a good machinist. Yeah.
Well, I don't know if he's living yet, Bill.
Work on cars and everything too.
Now, Lawrence Dury, he come home to tell me where he's living in.
Lafayette is it or someplace over there? Well, Lafayette I think. Well, Lafayette, I think.
Well, Lafayette, and, let me see, no, not Lafayette. Not far from New. Where Bunk is. New Iberia. New Iberia.
He'd been there. He's not right in that, he's up in the next town. No, no. He moved a little bit far.

Well, and Lawrence, well, there's two or three of them. There's two of them, I just not sure know if one Johnny's dead. Lawrence, I don't know if he's dead. Herbert, I don't know if he's dead. Eddie Garland, I don't know if he's living in there.
No, I saw Eddie Garland two years ago. Yeah. He's in pretty good health, he's still playing bass, but he's good. Yeah.
Well, George, I don't forget who he's playing with.
